articles.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
articles.content:
Researchers at La Brea Tar Pits have identified a previously unknown amphibian that lived in Ice Age Los Angeles. The extinct spadefoot toad, now named Spea labreae, represents the first new extinct amphibian species discovered from the famous fossil site.

The find is exceptionally rare. Only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has been discovered in North America (a tree frog from Florida). Although S. labreae was tiny compared with the mammoths and saber toothed cats associated with La Brea Tar Pits, its fossils could provide important clues about the climate and environmental changes that occurred near the end of the last ice age.

The species is described in theJournal of Vertebrate Paleontology. The discovery also highlights the new findings continuing to emerge from the Samuel Oschin Global Center for Ice Age Research at La Brea Tar Pits as the museum undergoes a historic transformation.

An Unexpected Discovery in an Old Fossil Collection

Lead author Dr. Alberto Cruz did not set out to discover a new species. He began studying the Tar Pits' relatively understudied reptile and amphibian collections while working there as a Postdoctoral Fellow. Cruz remains a Research Associate at La Brea Tar Pits and works full time as Researcher for Mexico's SECIHTI Centro de Investigación Paleontológica Quinametzin (CIPAQ), Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH).

"I'm really more of a paleoecologist, paleogeographer, not a taxonomist," says Dr. Cruz, who noticed unusual features in the Tar Pits specimens that distinguished S. labreae from known spadefoot toads.

At first, Cruz wondered whether the unusual bones belonged to an animal that had been sick or injured during its lifetime, which would make them an example of paleopathology. Comparisons with modern spadefoot toads eventually convinced him that the differences represented something else entirely.

"I reviewed and reviewed a lot of specimens until I was convinced. I thought, 'Oh my gosh, this is a new species.' This material is originally from the 1950s, but when you study it again, you can find gold in these specimens. It's very cool."

The fact that the fossils had been collected decades earlier shows how much scientific information can remain hidden in museum collections.

"It's a great example of how we're still finding new things at La Brea Tar Pits, even after a century of ongoing excavation and research," says Dr. Emily Lindsey, Curator and Excavation Site Director at the Samuel Oschin Global Center for Ice Age Research at La Brea Tar Pits. "There's definitely more to come."

Tiny Amphibians Can Reveal Ancient Climate

Large Ice Age mammals tend to attract the most attention at La Brea Tar Pits, but the much smaller reptiles and amphibians studied by Cruz can sometimes provide scientists with more detailed information about past climate and environmental conditions.

Amphibians generally do not travel long distances during their lives, and they are highly sensitive to changes in their surroundings. Those traits make them useful climate proxies. By determining where particular amphibians were present or absent, researchers can reconstruct environmental changes at a more local scale.

"If you change the environment, you change the vegetation, the climate is warmer or colder, it affects these animals directly," says Cruz.

Their usefulness comes with a major obstacle. Frogs, toads, and salamanders have delicate skeletons that do not fossilize easily, so their remains are uncommon in the fossil record outside asphaltic sites such as La Brea Tar Pits. That makes the discovery of a previously unknown small amphibian such as S. labreae especially remarkable.

The same fragility may also mean that many extinct reptiles and amphibians have disappeared from the fossil record entirely. Cruz and other researchers suspect that additional species once existed but left remains too delicate to survive long enough to be discovered.

Comparing Fossils With Modern Toads

To establish that the fossils represented a new species, Cruz closely examined amphibian bones from the La Brea Tar Pits collection, which had not received a detailed assessment in nearly 30 years. He documented differences in the shapes and sizes of the bones and compared the fossils with 80 specimens housed in the Herpetology Collections at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County and the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology at the University of California, Berkeley.

Those comparisons helped demonstrate that the La Brea fossils belonged to a distinct species of spadefoot toad rather than to an unusual individual of a known species.

Another Toad Reveals a Dramatically Different Los Angeles

The research produced another surprising discovery. Scientists identified the first known record of the Mexican burrowing toad, Rhinophrynus, in the southwestern United States.

These toads no longer live anywhere near Los Angeles. Their closest living populations are now nearly 2,500 km away in southern Mexico, indicating that the species once occupied a dramatically different geographic range.

That major shift in distribution, combined with the extinction of S. labreae, adds another piece to the complex history of environmental change as the last Ice Age came to an end. By examining how amphibians responded to those ancient changes, researchers may also gain insight into how similar animals could respond to human caused climate change today.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a new extinct amphibian species from the Ice Age in the La Brea Tar Pits has significant scientific value, providing important insights into past climate and environmental changes. This finding has broad implications for understanding environmental shifts and climate history, which can inform current climate change research. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful breakthrough in paleontology and climate science.
articles.personality_title: New Ice Age toad species discovered in La Brea Tar Pits fossils

articles.title: UK to turn cooler with rain after exceptional heat and dry spell
articles.summary: After and exceptional summer of heatwaves and drought, the weather will turn wetter and cooler this week, as Simon King explains
articles.content:
High pressure has been dominant this summer leading to hot and dry weather, particularly across England and Wales.

There's been no significant rain in southern England for around two months which has led water levels in our rivers and reservoirs to drop significantly. All of Wales and most of England are in drought.

However, through this week high pressure will be replaced by the influence of low pressure and more unsettled conditions.

Some light rain is likely on Monday, mostly across northern areas of the UK.

Into Tuesday and Wednesady this will turn heavier and start to move into southern England.

While rain is therefore finally going to fall across the south, it may become more showery. This means the exact location and distribution of rainfall is still uncertain.

And while of course any rain will be welcome, it won't bring much improvement to conditions.

It will take weeks of above average rainfall into the autumn to make any significant changes to the drought.

However, it is likely to make a big difference to the emergency services who have been battling against the extreme weather and wildfires over the last few weeks.

The fire severity index —how severe a fire could be, should one to start — will come down to low or moderate, according to forecasts from Natural England and the Met Office.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant weather change bringing rain and cooler conditions after an exceptional heatwave and drought, which will help reduce wildfire risks and aid emergency services. Although it won't immediately end the drought, this shift has meaningful positive environmental and societal impacts.
articles.personality_title: UK weather shifts to cooler, wetter conditions after long heatwave
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – This summer, the UK experienced very hot and dry weather, especially in England and Wales. There was almost no rain in southern England for about two months, causing rivers and reservoirs to have much less water. Most of England and all of Wales are now in drought.

**What happened** – This week, the weather is changing. The high pressure that kept the weather hot and dry is moving away. Low pressure is bringing cooler air and more rain. Light rain started on Monday in northern UK areas, and heavier rain moved south on Tuesday and Wednesday. The rain may come in showers, so it might not fall evenly everywhere.

**Impact** – The rain and cooler weather will help reduce the risk of wildfires, which have been a big problem during the dry summer. Emergency services, like firefighters, will find it easier to manage fires now. However, the rain won’t be enough to fix the drought quickly because it will take many weeks of above-average rain to refill rivers and reservoirs.

**What's next step** – In the coming weeks, weather experts will watch if more rain continues through autumn. If it does, the drought could improve over time. Meanwhile, the fire risk is expected to stay low or moderate, which means fewer dangerous fires might start.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After a long dry and hot summer, the UK is finally seeing cooler weather and rain that will lower fire risks and help emergency teams, even if drought recovery will take longer.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le temps au Royaume-Uni devient plus frais et humide après une longue période de chaleur
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Cet été, le Royaume-Uni a connu un temps très chaud et sec, surtout en Angleterre et au Pays de Galles. Il n’a presque pas plu dans le sud de l’Angleterre pendant environ deux mois, ce qui a beaucoup réduit le niveau des rivières et des réservoirs. La majeure partie de l’Angleterre et tout le Pays de Galles sont maintenant en situation de sécheresse.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Cette semaine, le temps change. La haute pression qui maintenait le temps chaud et sec s’éloigne. Une basse pression amène de l’air plus frais et de la pluie. Une légère pluie a commencé lundi dans le nord du Royaume-Uni, puis la pluie plus forte est arrivée dans le sud mardi et mercredi. La pluie pourrait tomber par averses, donc elle ne sera pas répartie de manière uniforme.

**Impact** – La pluie et le temps plus frais vont aider à réduire les risques d’incendies, qui ont été un gros problème cet été. Les services d’urgence, comme les pompiers, auront plus de facilité à gérer les incendies. Cependant, cette pluie ne suffira pas à résoudre rapidement la sécheresse, car il faudra plusieurs semaines de pluie supérieure à la normale pour remplir les rivières et réservoirs.

**Prochaine étape** – Dans les semaines à venir, les experts surveilleront si la pluie continue en automne. Si c’est le cas, la sécheresse pourrait s’améliorer avec le temps. En attendant, le risque d’incendie devrait rester faible ou modéré, ce qui signifie qu’il pourrait y avoir moins d’incendies dangereux.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après un long été chaud et sec, le Royaume-Uni connaît enfin un temps plus frais et de la pluie qui réduiront les risques d’incendies et aideront les équipes d’urgence, même si la sécheresse mettra plus de temps à disparaître.
articles.personality_title_es: El clima en Reino Unido se vuelve más fresco y húmedo tras una larga ola de calor
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Este verano, el Reino Unido tuvo un clima muy caluroso y seco, especialmente en Inglaterra y Gales. No ha llovido casi nada en el sur de Inglaterra durante cerca de dos meses, lo que ha hecho que los niveles de ríos y embalses bajen mucho. La mayor parte de Inglaterra y todo Gales están en sequía.

**Qué pasó** – Esta semana, el clima está cambiando. La alta presión que mantenía el tiempo caluroso y seco se está alejando. La baja presión trae aire más fresco y lluvia. La lluvia ligera comenzó el lunes en el norte del Reino Unido y la lluvia más fuerte llegó al sur el martes y miércoles. La lluvia puede venir en chubascos, por lo que no caerá por igual en todas partes.

**Impacto** – La lluvia y el clima más fresco ayudarán a reducir el riesgo de incendios, que han sido un gran problema durante el verano seco. Los servicios de emergencia, como los bomberos, tendrán más facilidad para controlar los incendios. Sin embargo, esta lluvia no será suficiente para acabar con la sequía rápidamente, porque se necesitarán varias semanas de lluvia por encima de lo normal para llenar los ríos y embalses.

**Próximo paso** – En las próximas semanas, los expertos en clima observarán si la lluvia continúa durante el otoño. Si es así, la sequía podría mejorar con el tiempo. Mientras tanto, se espera que el riesgo de incendio se mantenga bajo o moderado, lo que significa que podrían empezar menos incendios peligrosos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Tras un largo verano seco y caluroso, el Reino Unido finalmente tiene un clima más fresco y lluvias que reducirán el riesgo de incendios y ayudarán a los equipos de emergencia, aunque la sequía tardará más en mejorar.
